problem_framing.rationale: The document answers the question exactly as posed (whether to raise, and how) on the title and summary slides. It uses both stated objectives as explicit criteria: the 15% growth target is tested in an ARR bridge ($97.0M, +12.8%, $1.9M gap) and NRR above 100% is checked for each option. It applies the renewal-timing and enterprise-contract constraints directly in the sizing. It identifies early what the answer turns on: cohort versus rate effect, pricing power by segment, and the true size of the $10.3M. The only oddity is slide 3, which frames the author's own starting hypothesis rather than the CFO's, though the CFO and CEO views are both addressed directly elsewhere.

storyline_coherence.rationale: The governing thought answers the question, the four summary points map onto the four sections (diagnosis, pricing power, value, plan), and nearly every title is a claim its slide supports; the titles alone give the argument. Three flaws keep it from a 5. Slide 3 is a process narrative that repeats later content. Slides 12, 13 and 15 overlap on the plan, and slide 14 repeats caveats made elsewhere. Slide 6's title ('every signal points the same way') overstates, given that slide 4 flags an unexplained rise in mid-market churn and the mid-market test covered new sign-ups only.

evidence_and_reasoning.rationale: I re-derived the key numbers and they hold: promo churn 4.9% and 56% of churners; blended logo churn 1.7% to 2.6% and ARR-weighted 0.8% to 1.2%; the $10.32M to $7.566M waterfall (2.466 not renewing, 0.288 cap); 12-month retention factors; segment net gains (0.77, -0.13, 2.90/2.43, 0.65/0.59); break-evens of 9.1%, 10.7% and 7.4%; the 2023 cumulative loss of 3.6%; the activation decomposition (1.35%, 2.9%, about 30%); and the bridge to $97.0M. All critical evidence is used, including evidence against the answer (2023 precedent, new-sign-up caveat, mid-market churn up). It also catches that the 34% survey figure differs from the mix-implied 37%. The elasticities are transparent, labelled as assumptions and stress-tested. Remaining flaws are minor: 'NRR 112–114% in every option' is wrong for option A (109.3%), the win-rate fall is attributed causally to Inkwell's $9 plan, and 19% for all SMB churners is used as the core-SMB baseline. None is material.

strategic_judgment.rationale: The recommendation is clear, differs by segment and follows from the analysis: +10% for mid-market and uncapped enterprise, 7% on capped contracts, hold SMB pending a test with a July gate, and exclude the promo cohort. Four options are compared on base and downside ARR, growth against the 15% target and main risk, and the document states what is given up against the CFO's plan (about $1.2M base, equal downside). It gives quantified guardrails and stop rules (mid-market churn above 1.2% against a break-even near 1.55%; SMB test extra churn above 0.5pp). It is candid that pricing alone misses 15% and assigns the gap to Sales. It reconciles the CFO and CEO views, rejects the 'halve churn' claim with a reason, and avoids all five traps. Small gaps: a lower-priced SMB tier against Inkwell is only gestured at ('review packaging'), and customer trust at renewal is barely discussed.

clarity_and_concision.rationale: The answer is on the title and summary slides, the language is plain and derivations are footnoted. But at 17 slides and about 4,000 words it is somewhat longer than the decision needs: slide 3 is dispensable, slides 12, 13 and 15 overlap, and several slides are dense. Figures such as 4.17837 are probably an extraction artefact and are not penalised.

unsupported_claims.quote: SMB: Inkwell's $9 plan has cut Palisade's win rate from 51% to 38%.
unsupported_claims.why: The pack shows the win rate fell in deals where Inkwell was considered; attributing the fall causally to the $9 plan is plausible but not established.

unsupported_claims.quote: Churn 0.2%, NRR 118%, high switching costs; contracts set the ceiling
unsupported_claims.why: Switching costs are not stated in the pack; this is inferred from customers citing integrations and the audit trail as reasons to stay.

unsupported_claims.quote: The share of these churners citing price fell from 19% to 18%, so Inkwell has not yet hurt retention.
unsupported_claims.why: The 19% is for all SMB churners in H1 2025, not specifically the non-promo group, and the inference about Inkwell rests on a small survey difference; it is directionally reasonable but stated more firmly than the data allow.

unsupported_claims.quote: Better onboarding explains only ~30% of the promo cohort's excess churn; the rest is a reaction to the discount ending
unsupported_claims.why: The 30% depends on assuming the 3× activation ratio applies identically within both cohorts. The residual is 'not explained' in the document's own chart but is attributed to the discount ending in the title; timing and survey evidence support this but do not prove it.

numerical_errors.correct: Option A (hold all prices) gives 93.98/86 = 109.3%, the trailing NRR the document itself reports in the appendix; 112–114% applies only to the price-rise options.

recommendation.summary: Raise by segment: +10% for mid-market and uncapped enterprise from January 2027 renewals (7% on capped enterprise contracts). Hold SMB list prices in H1 and test +8% on new sign-ups and a renewal group, with a July rollout only if churn and win-rate gates pass. Exclude the promo cohort from any rise, stop 50%-off offers and fund activation outreach. Have Sales commit about $1.9M of new-customer ARR to reach 15%, and restate the board churn metric.
recommendation.rationale: The recommendation meets all four defensibility criteria. It separates the mix effect from the rate effect (promo 4.9% against core 2.1%). It reconciles the CFO and CEO views (CFO 'half right': core customers are not leaving over price, the promo cohort is). It corrects the $10.3M to $7.6M eligible and about $4.2M net. It differentiates pricing by segment, with a staged SMB test and quantified guardrails.

hypothesis_handling.rationale: The CFO's flat 12% / $10.3M / 'onboarding, not price' position is revised, not adopted or dismissed. The sizing is cut to $7.6M eligible and $4.2M net. The diagnosis is called 'half right': core SMB churn is flat, but the promo cohort leaves over price when the discount ends. The uniform increase is replaced by a segmented one. The CEO's concern is addressed by showing the churn rise is a cohort effect while SMB remains exposed to Inkwell, hence the test gate. The document also challenges the Customer Success 'halve churn' claim and the undefined dashboard metric, and caveats the new-sign-up test. Two causal attributions are stated more firmly than the evidence allows: Inkwell 'cut' the win rate, and the unexplained churn residual is a reaction to the discount ending.

output.overall_comment: This is very strong work: weighted score 4.65 (framing 5, coherence 4, evidence 5, judgment 5, clarity 4). Every key calculation I re-derived matches the pack and the answer key, including promo churn of 4.9%, the mix decomposition, blended and ARR-weighted churn, $7.57M eligible uplift and the 10.7% break-even. The document goes beyond the key with a net-of-churn sizing by segment under base and downside cases, an activation decomposition of promo churn, and an ARR bridge against the 15% target. It reconciles the CFO and CEO views, avoids all five traps, and lands on a segmented, gated plan with quantified stop rules. The weaknesses are minor: some redundancy and length (slides 3 and 12–15), an overstated title on slide 6, one small NRR misstatement for the hold option, and a few causal claims stated more firmly than the evidence supports. It also gives limited attention to an SMB packaging or lower-tier response to Inkwell and to customer trust at renewal.
